title: Medicine and fasting
hook: doctors and scholars on fasting with illness

segments.voice: Yesterday, science and faith, and the study of the natural world as a way of reading signs. Your line was science reads signs. Did you stop over one small wonder? Today, the body doing the reading. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

A clinic waiting room, a few weeks before Ramadan. A woman with diabetes is holding a question she has carried all year: can I fast this time? Her doctor has an answer about blood sugar. Her imam has an answer about the law. What she wants is the two of them in the same room. That room, doctors and scholars talking together about fasting and illness, is where today starts. And the Qur'an had already made space for her, in the very passage that commands the fast.
screen: `A QUESTION BEFORE RAMADAN.` → `A DOCTOR AND AN IMAM.` → `THE SAME PASSAGE.`

segments.voice: The verse that sets the fast carries its own exception. In Surah al-Baqarah, Pickthall's translation reads: "(for) him who is sick among you, or on a journey, (the same) number of other days." So the person who is ill and doesn't fast isn't breaking the rule. They're following it. The days can be made up later. The same verse speaks of a ransom, feeding a person in need, which scholars apply to someone who can't make the days up at all, like a person with a lasting illness. The next verse gives the reason in plain words: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." Then the hadith add a second thread. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, hears of a companion who fasts every day and prays all night, and tells him to ease off, because, in paraphrase, your body has a right over you. And in Sunan Abu Dawud he tells people to seek treatment, since Allah has not made a disease without making a remedy for it. Put those side by side and you have today's line: health is a trust. The body isn't simply yours to spend down. It's held on someone's behalf. So the question in the clinic isn't how tough are you. It's what will this do to you. Some scholars hold that the advice of a trustworthy doctor can settle it. Where they differ is in the gray cases: how sick is sick enough, and whether an inhaler or an injection breaks the fast. Those questions are why the doctor and the imam keep meeting.
screen: `THE EXCEPTION IS IN THE VERSE.` · `ALLAH DESIRETH FOR YOU EASE.` · `YOUR BODY HAS A RIGHT OVER YOU.` · `A DOCTOR AND A SCHOLAR, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take your health seriously for two minutes. Settle, and breathe. Start at your feet and move slowly upward, noticing where you're tired, sore or tight, without fixing anything yet. Then ask one honest question: what have I been putting off? A checkup. A prescription. Sleep. Water. A conversation with a doctor. Name one. If you pray, you can hold your body in mind as something entrusted to you. If you don't, simply hold the one thing you named. The bell holds the time.
Medicine and fasting. The fast of Ramadan carries its own exception for the sick, and the hadith tell people to seek a cure. Today's word.
Your line: health is a trust. Today, do the one thing you named: book it, take it, drink it, or ask about it. Tomorrow, the environment. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims who are ill or traveling may leave the Ramadan fast and make up the days later; someone who cannot make them up may feed a person in need instead, and some consult both a doctor and a scholar before the month begins.

original.note: Arabic: the fasting, the word the Qur'an uses when it prescribes the fast (2:183).

trapdoor: what you thought: fasting is a test of how tough you are.
what it means: the fast comes with its own exception. the sick make up the days later, because Allah desires ease, not hardship.
what a scholar hears: 2:184–185 on the sick, the traveler and the ransom; the body's right in al-Bukhari; seeking treatment in Abu Dawud; and open questions about injections and inhalers.
